newsitem.title: CHINA: Hopewell faces biggest risk in railway.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell faces biggest risk in railway.

text.p: Gordon Wu has tempted fate before and won, but this time the Hong Kong infrastructure developer may be facing his most serious financial crisis ever.

The Thai government has given Wu's Hopewell Holding Ltd until the end of the month to prove it can finance and finish on time its US$3.2 billion Bangkok mass transit project, in which the company has already invested US$560 million of its own money.
Wu, the Hong Kong-born engineer, visionary of grand schemes and risk taker par excellence, has pulled the company through some tough times in the past decade, but can he do it this time?
Many analysts fear Hopewell, which laid highways across southern China and built power plants in the Philippines, may be gridlocked with the Bangkok Elevated Rail Train System (BERTS).

"The viabilities and the way it was conceived were too optimistic from the beginning," said analyst Michael Green at Salomon Brothers of the project. "Clearly there is a mismatch between the conception and the reality."

Hopewell has gone where few private sector contractors have gone before -- into the world of major infrastructural development projects, usually reserved for governments and supra-national financial institutions.

"Gordon Wu has been rewarded for his development style and for taking on the risks that he took, that other people didn't, such as Shajiao B and his success in the Philippines," one analyst said. "A lot of people won't take those risks."
"But he has also got himself in trouble in the Tanjung Jati and the BERTS projects," said the analyst.
Probably Hopewell's biggest success stories was the establishment and public listing of its former subsidiary, Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA).
CEPA held the group's power plant construction projects, building coal-fired and gas-fired power plants in China and the Philippines, and with plans for others throughout Asia.
The company took on these large projects using only private capital, thus greatly increasing the project and investment risks involved, said analysts.

But Hopewell last year agreed to sell two-thirds of its 60-percent stake in CEPA to Southern Co Inc of the United States in a deal that valued CEPA at US$3.2 billion. Analysts said the deal was driven by Hopewell's need to reduce debt.
Last week Hopewell sold its remaining 20 percent holding in exchange for CEPA's 80 percent interest in the Tanjung Jati power station project in Indonesia and US$150 million in cash.

Analysts said Hopewell needed the cash, while CEPA managing director Raymond Hill recently told Reuters that, unlike Hopewell, the new Southern-owned CEPA could not live with the uncertainties and the higher risk elements of Tanjung Jati.

Hopewell's biggest project and biggest investment risk to date is the Bangkok mass transit project, involving a toll road, an elevated train system, and the upgrading of part of the existing state railway network in Bangkok.

The US$3.2 billion project, originally due to be completed by 1999, involves construction of 60 km (37.5 miles) of multi-level railways and highways, and the company said it has financed the entire project itself so far.
"The company may have bit off more than it can chew," said Salomon's Green.
The Thai government wants the first phase of the project to be completed before the Asian Games are held in Bangkok in December 1998, but the project has been dogged by delays.

"The project has had many delays over the years due to frequent changes in government and design changes, including width of the toll road and interfaces with other government projects as well as land issues," said Hopewell in a statement issued before a key meeting with Thai government last Friday.
Thailand's economic malaise and the recent drop in the value of the local currency threw up further roadblocks, and Hopewell said banks may have to reassess project financing.
Wu has been typically confident, insisting financing was no problem and pushing the Thai government to allow higher fares to cover increased costs and to quickly deliver the needed land.

"You deliver all the land, you agree on the fare structure, and I'll sign the deal with the financing people, we'll get the money, we'll finish the job, and not a damn day before," he told reporters in Hong Kong last Monday.
But now Bangkok wants the Hong Kong risk taker to lay down his cards first.
